categories.label: Action
categories.tagline: Get up. Run around. Burn off the snacks.

categories.label: Imagination
categories.tagline: Roleplay, improv, retelling — Scripture made vivid.

categories.label: Mind
categories.tagline: Memory drills, riddles, puzzles. Brain warm-ups.

categories.label: Icebreakers
categories.tagline: Warm up the room when half the group doesn't know each other.

games.t: FOUR CORNERS · The Decision Game
games.h: Each corner is an opinion. Defend yours with your body.
steps: Label the four corners of your room: Strongly Agree, Agree, Disagree, Strongly Disagree.
Read out a statement related to your study — like "Forgiveness should always come before justice."
Everyone walks to the corner that matches what they really think.
Pick one person from each corner to say why they're standing there. No debating yet — just listening.
games.why: Bodies betray real opinions. People who would never speak up in a circle will plant their feet in a corner. The walking is the conversation.

games.t: SARDINES · Reverse Hide and Seek
games.h: One person hides. Everyone else finds them — and joins them in hiding.
steps: Pick one person to hide. Everyone else closes their eyes and counts to 60.
Everyone scatters and searches. When you find the hider, you don't shout — you silently squeeze in next to them.
The hiding spot fills up like sardines in a can. Last person to find the group becomes the next hider.
No talking once you've joined the hidden cluster. Silent giggling allowed.
games.why: The whole house becomes a game. People stop checking their phones when they're crammed behind a couch with five friends, trying not to laugh.

games.t: WORD ON FIRE · Silent Charades, Bible Edition
games.h: One word. Sixty seconds. No sounds. Welcome to the chaos.
steps: Everyone writes 5 Bible-related words or scenes on slips of paper. Fold them up, put them in a bowl.
Split into two teams.
One player at a time pulls a slip and acts it out — no talking, no pointing at objects, no sounds.
Their team has 60 seconds to guess. Right guess = point. Pass if stuck.
games.why: You'll never forget the time someone tried to act out 'Nebuchadnezzar.' Shared physical comedy bonds a group faster than any discussion.

games.t: PROPHETS, KINGS, FOOLS · The Biblical Rock-Paper-Scissors
games.h: Three roles, one winner. The whole group plays at once.
steps: Three roles: Prophet (raises arms), King (crosses arms on chest), Fool (sticks tongue out).
Prophet beats King (truth to power). King beats Fool (authority over folly). Fool beats Prophet (the world rejects truth).
Everyone walks around the room. On "Go!" everyone strikes a pose simultaneously.
If you match your pose with someone, look at each other — winning role advances, losing role sits down.
games.why: Pure absurdity wrapped in a real biblical idea. Kids and adults laugh at the same things here.

games.t: STATUE PROCLAIM · Freeze on the Verse
games.h: Dance until the verse drops. Freeze the second it lands.
steps: Pick one person to be the Caller. The Caller reads a Bible verse out loud.
Everyone else moves freely — dance, walk, jog in place — while the Caller reads.
The instant the Caller says the last word of the verse, EVERYONE FREEZES.
Anyone who moves after the freeze sits down for that round.
games.why: Scripture as a physical signal. The verse becomes a thing your body learns, not just words your ears process.

games.t: BIBLE TAG · Saved by the Verse
games.h: Get tagged? You're frozen. Recite a verse? You're free.
steps: Pick 1-2 people to be It. Everyone else scatters.
If you're tagged, you freeze in place.
You can be unfrozen by another player running up to you and reciting any verse out loud. Even one they made up the meaning of.
It can't tag the person who's reciting. They have one verse-length grace period.
games.why: Memory verses become escape tokens. Suddenly memorizing scripture is the coolest skill in the room.

games.t: THE GREAT EXODUS · Whole-Room Relay
games.h: Cross the Red Sea, gather the manna, reach the promised land — as a team.
steps: Set up 3-4 "stations" around the room: Red Sea (crawl under chairs), Manna (collect crumpled paper balls into a bowl), Wilderness (hop on one foot for 20 seconds), Promised Land (group hug at the finish).
Split into teams of 4-6.
Each team member tackles one station before tagging the next teammate.
First team to finish the journey wins.
games.why: You're living the Exodus instead of reading about it. The grumbling, the relief, the celebration — your body learns the story arc.

games.t: LIONS' DEN · One vs. the Group
games.h: One Daniel. Many lions. Cross the room without getting touched.
steps: Pick one player to be Daniel. Everyone else is a lion.
Mark a start line and finish line about 20 feet apart. Lions stand in the middle zone.
Lions can ONLY move when Daniel's back is turned. Like Red Light Green Light, but Daniel decides when to look.
Daniel tries to walk from start to finish backwards (so the lions can't move easily).
games.why: The Bible story has tension. This game has tension. Same root emotion, different mechanism.

games.t: JONAH'S RUN · Tag with a Twist
games.h: Run from God's call. Get caught. Discover you actually wanted to go.
steps: One person is "the call." Everyone else is Jonah.
The call walks (not runs) toward Jonahs. Jonahs flee.
When a Jonah is tagged, they freeze for 5 seconds, then JOIN the call — now walking together, hand-in-hand or shoulder-to-shoulder.
The call line grows. Last Jonah free is the next "call."
games.why: Watch people physically experience what running from God feels like — and then notice the relief when they're caught.

games.t: ANGELS & PHARISEES · Hidden Roles
games.h: Werewolf, but biblical. Find the Pharisees before they outvote the Angels.
steps: Write roles on slips of paper: 2 Pharisees, 1 Prophet, the rest are Angels. Shuffle and hand them out face down.
Night round: everyone closes eyes. "Pharisees, wake up — pick someone to silence." (Moderator notes who.) "Prophet, wake up — point at one player — moderator nods yes if they're a Pharisee."
Day round: moderator reveals who was silenced (they're out). Discussion. Everyone votes someone to "call out." That person's role is revealed and they're out.
Angels win when both Pharisees are out. Pharisees win when they equal or outnumber Angels.
games.why: Deception, defense, deduction. Same skills the early church needed. Plus everyone gets really into it.

games.t: SHEEP & SHEPHERD · Trust Walk
games.h: Eyes closed. One voice guides you across the room. Don't bump into the furniture.
steps: Pair up. One is the shepherd, one is the sheep.
The sheep closes their eyes. The shepherd guides them across the room using only their voice — no touching.
Add obstacles: chairs, pillows, other pairs walking through. Make it spicy.
Switch roles. Pair switches partners. Run it 4-5 times.
games.why: John 10 hits different after you've literally followed someone's voice through chaos. The trust is in your body now.

games.t: THE GREAT FLOOD · Stepping Stones
games.h: The floor is the flood. The pages of newspaper are dry ground. Cross without touching water.
steps: Hand each team 5-7 sheets of newspaper. Mark a start line and finish line about 15 feet apart.
The floor between is the flood — touch it and you restart.
Teams must move all members across by placing newspapers on the floor and stepping on them.
Catch: a newspaper not under a foot floats away (the leader picks it up).
games.why: Forces teamwork without conversation. Watch leaders emerge, watch quiet planners get loud.

games.t: JERICHO MARCH · Silence, Then Shout
games.h: Six laps in silence. Seventh lap, you scream. The walls fall.
steps: Designate the center of the room as Jericho. The group walks around it in a circle.
Six laps — total silence. Anyone who talks does pushups (or sits out a round).
On lap seven, the leader shouts "SHOUT!" — and everyone screams whatever they want as loud as they can.
Stack chairs in the middle beforehand. Let one chair 'fall' on the shout.
games.why: The silence before the shout makes the shout cathartic. People feel the weight of obedience and the release of breakthrough — without you having to explain it.

games.t: BURNING BUSH · Freeze on the Voice
games.h: Run free until a voice calls your name. Then stop, listen, and answer.
steps: Everyone moves around the room — walk, jog, skip — except one person, the Voice.
The Voice randomly calls a player's name. That player must freeze immediately and say 'Here I am.'
Anyone who doesn't freeze in time or says something else sits out a round.
Switch the Voice every minute. Last 3 standing win.
games.why: Trains the ear to recognize being called. Surprisingly emotional after a few rounds.

games.t: EXODUS ESCAPE · Group Obstacle Race
games.h: Egypt is the start. Promised land is the finish. The whole group moves together — or no one does.
steps: Set up 3-4 obstacles around the space: crawl under a table, jump over a pillow line, hop on one foot through a "wilderness."
The whole group must do each obstacle in order. The slowest person sets the pace.
Rule: no one moves to the next obstacle until everyone clears the current one.
Time the run. Run it again. Try to beat your time.
games.why: Frustration becomes patience. Faster people learn to wait, slower people feel the team behind them. Just like the wilderness.

games.t: CROWN OR THORN · Snap Decision Sprint
games.h: Two corners: 'Crown' or 'Thorn.' Hear the question, pick a corner, run.
steps: Mark two corners: Crown and Thorn (or Heaven/Hell, Light/Dark, etc).
Read a quick "would you rather" or moral pop-quiz statement. Examples: "Do the right thing alone vs. do the wrong thing with friends." "Power vs. peace."
Everyone has 3 seconds to RUN to their corner.
Last to arrive in either corner sits out next round. Last 3 standing win.
games.why: No time to overthink. Your body picks before your brain rationalizes. That gap is the lesson.

games.t: DAVID'S SLING · Paper-Ball Precision
games.h: Five paper balls. One target. Knock the giant down.
steps: Crumple 5 paper balls per player. Set up a "giant" — a stack of cups, a chair with a hat, a labeled paper plate.
From 10 feet away, each player throws 5 balls one at a time. Knock parts down for points.
Tournament style: top 2 from each round move on. Final shootout from 15 feet.
games.why: Quiet kid + good aim = champion. The game rewards focus over loudness, which Bible study often does too.

games.t: STORM ON GALILEE · Boat Balance
games.h: You're all in the boat. Captain shouts "STORM" — sway. "JESUS WALKS" — kneel.
steps: Everyone stands in a tight cluster pretending to be in a boat. One leader is the Captain.
Captain calls commands: "STORM" (everyone sways), "STILL" (freeze), "BAIL" (mime scooping water), "JESUS WALKS" (everyone kneels), "PETER STEPS OUT" (one foot in front of the other in place).
Whoever does the wrong command sits down. Get faster.
Last person standing is the new Captain.
games.why: Like Simon Says, but with built-in story. Kids GET this. Adults laugh at themselves for forgetting which command was which.

games.t: THE GOOD SHEPHERD · Find the Voice
games.h: Three shepherds. Twelve sheep. Only one shepherd's voice will lead you home.
steps: Pick 3 shepherds. Each picks a unique phrase (e.g. "this way, this way" / "come along now" / "follow me home").
Assign each remaining player to one shepherd in secret. Everyone closes eyes.
Shepherds spread out across the room. Sheep listen and walk slowly toward their assigned shepherd, eyes closed.
Shepherds keep saying their phrase. If a sheep arrives at the wrong shepherd, that shepherd nudges them away.
games.why: John 10:27 lived out. Some people will literally feel emotional finding the right voice in the dark.

games.t: RACE TO BETHLEHEM · The Wheelbarrow Relay
games.h: One pushes, one walks on hands. Wheelbarrow your way to the manger.
steps: Pair up by similar height/weight. One is the wheelbarrow (hands on floor), the other holds their ankles (the driver).
Set a start line and "Bethlehem" finish line 20 feet apart.
Wheelbarrow your way across. Switch roles. Run back. First team done wins.
games.why: The "drivers" learn what gentle leadership feels like (push too hard, the wheelbarrow falls). The "wheelbarrows" learn to trust.

games.t: TEMPLE COURTS · Freeze on Prayer
games.h: Walk freely until someone prays out loud. Freeze, listen, then move again.
steps: Everyone moves around the room casually — talking, joking, drifting.
Pick a pre-chosen Prayer. At any moment, the Prayer raises both arms and says a short prayer out loud (5-10 seconds).
Everyone freezes. Eyes closed if they want. Listen.
When the prayer ends, everyone moves again. Repeat 4-5 times with different Prayers.
games.why: Public prayer becomes a normal interruption in the day — not a Sunday-only ritual. Practice for life.

games.t: JOSEPH'S COAT · Color-Tag
games.h: Multiple safe zones, multiple "it" players, color-coded chaos.
steps: Mark 4 safe zones around the room with different colors (use construction paper, sticky notes).
Pick 2-3 "brothers" to be It. They try to tag everyone else.
Players are safe in any colored zone — but can only stay 5 seconds before they must move.
Tagged players become Brothers. Game ends when only Joseph is left.
games.why: Movement chaos with strategy. The "Joseph" who lasts longest is usually the most generous about helping others escape — fitting.

games.t: EZEKIEL'S BONES · From Lying to Standing
games.h: Lie down 'dead.' At the command, rise. Last team to assemble wins.
steps: Split into teams. Each team lies on the floor in a pile — totally limp, totally "dead."
Leader yells: "DRY BONES, HEAR THE WORD OF THE LORD!"
Teams must, in order: 1) sit up (sinews), 2) stand (flesh), 3) link arms (breath), 4) shout "WE LIVE!"
Each phase must be done together. If anyone breaks order, restart that team.
games.why: Ezekiel 37 is theater. This game lets you BE the theater. Hard not to feel the weight of resurrection language by the end.

games.t: THE WALL · Pass the Stone
games.h: Human chain. Pass the stone. No drops. Rebuild the wall.
steps: Form a single-file line across the room. Hand the first person an object (a ball, a stuffed animal, a real rock).
Pass it down the line — only with hands.
Twist: each round you can only use a different body part: just elbows, just under the chin, just on the back of your hand.
If you drop it, the object goes back to the start. Time how fast you can clear a round.
games.why: Nehemiah-style cooperation. Every person matters or the wall doesn't rise.

games.t: PETER WALKS · Eyes-Closed Step-Out
games.h: Eyes closed. Hand of a friend. Step into the unknown.
steps: Pair up. One is Peter (eyes closed), one is Jesus (sees everything).
Jesus stands across the room. Peter must walk to Jesus with eyes closed — using only ambient sense and Jesus calling them by name.
No physical touch unless Peter is about to walk into something.
Switch roles. Try it again with obstacles in the way.
games.why: Most people will open their eyes mid-walk. They learn something about their own faith without anyone preaching at them.

games.t: PARABLE REMIX · Retell with a Twist
games.h: Tell the Prodigal Son like a heist movie. Watch the truth survive.
steps: Pick a parable everyone knows — Prodigal Son, Good Samaritan, Lost Sheep.
Spin a genre wheel (write 8 on paper): heist movie, romcom, sci-fi, true crime, mockumentary, cooking show, sports broadcast, horror.
In small groups (2-4 people), reframe the parable in that genre. 10 minutes to plan.
Each group performs theirs as a 60-second skit.
games.why: Genre is wallpaper. The truth of the parable is structure. You only see structure when you change the wallpaper.

games.t: EMPTY CHAIR · Talk to the Character
games.h: One empty chair. One Bible character sitting in it. Ask anything.
steps: Place an empty chair in the middle of the circle. Pick a Bible character — Peter, Mary, Job, Esther.
One volunteer "becomes" that character and sits in the chair.
The rest of the group asks them anything. Why did you do it? What were you scared of? What do you wish you knew?
The volunteer answers in-character — making up details where Scripture is silent is OK and encouraged.
games.why: Imagining a character forces empathy. You stop reading them as a historical figure and start hearing them as a person.

games.t: BIBLE NEWS · Live Report from the Passage
games.h: You are a reporter at the Red Sea. The crossing just happened. Go live.
steps: Pick a passage with action — Red Sea, walls of Jericho, feeding of 5000, calming the storm.
Assign roles: anchor, on-the-scene reporter, eyewitness 1, eyewitness 2, expert analyst.
Each group puts on a 3-minute "news segment" covering the event from those angles.
After: which 'reporter' got the heart of it right? Which one missed?
games.why: Reporting forces "what would I have actually noticed?" Most of us breeze past the miracle. The news format makes us slow down.

games.t: THE LOST SHEEP · One Leaves, Everyone Notices
games.h: One person quietly leaves the room. How long until you notice?
steps: Everyone forms a circle and starts a casual conversation about anything.
One person — pre-selected by a coin flip — quietly steps out at any time during the conversation.
The conversation continues. The group must notice they're gone WITHOUT looking around the circle.
When someone notices, they say nothing — they walk out and bring the lost sheep back.
games.why: Most of us are surrounded by people who are slipping away unnoticed. This game lives in your gut for a week after.

games.t: SHADOW SCRIPTURES · Silent Reenactment
games.h: Tell a Bible story with only body language. No words. No sounds.
steps: Split into groups of 3-5. Each group picks a Bible story (or draws one from a hat).
They have 10 minutes to plan a 90-second silent reenactment — no words, no sounds.
The rest of the group guesses the story.
Tip: gestures should be big, characters should be clearly differentiated, the climax should be the most dramatic moment.
games.why: Stripped of dialogue, the emotional beats of the story become obvious. People often discover what a passage is REALLY about.

games.t: PSALM SLAM · Co-Write a Psalm
games.h: Three minutes. Five voices. One brand-new psalm.
steps: Pick a feeling for the psalm: grief, gratitude, anger at injustice, awe, longing, repentance.
Pass a notebook around the circle. Each person writes ONE line, then passes it.
No reading the previous lines — just continue what feels right.
After 5 passes (or when the notebook says STOP), read the whole psalm out loud, together.
games.why: The Psalms feel timeless because they're honest. When YOUR group writes one honestly, it joins the tradition.

games.t: ALTERNATE ENDINGS · What If Jonah Said Yes?
games.h: Rewind the story. Change one decision. Live with the new ending.
steps: Pick a story with a clear pivotal choice — Jonah's run, Peter's denial, Mary's yes, Judas's betrayal.
In small groups, imagine: what if they made the OTHER choice? What changes? What stays the same?
Each group acts out their alternate ending in 2 minutes.
After: why did the actual story have to go the way it did? What's the difference between God's plan and human choices?
games.why: Counterfactuals make the real story feel inevitable in a new way. You see what was at stake.

games.t: WHO AM I? · The Bible Character Whisper
games.h: A name on your forehead. Ask yes/no questions. Guess who you are.
steps: Each person writes a Bible character on a sticky note. Pass it RIGHT — that person sticks it on the forehead of the next person without looking at it.
Now you have a name on your head you can't see. Everyone else can see it.
Take turns asking yes/no questions: 'Am I in the Old Testament?' 'Did I do something heroic?' 'Am I a woman?'
First to guess their identity wins. Keep going until everyone's figured out theirs.
games.why: You realize how much you actually know — or don't know — about the Bible's cast of characters.

games.t: BIBLE OPERA · Sing Every Line
games.h: Read a Bible chapter — but every line must be sung. Absolutely no talking.
steps: Pick a short, dramatic passage — David & Goliath, the prodigal son's return, Mary at the tomb.
Assign parts. Everyone reads their lines — but they must SING. Any melody. Make it up.
The narrator can sing dramatically. Characters can sing operatically. Bonus points for harmonies.
Don't try to be good. Try to commit fully.
games.why: Singing slows you down. Words you'd skim become words you must inhabit. Plus, everyone leaves laughing.

games.t: EMOJI GOSPEL · The Story in 5 Symbols
games.h: Tell a whole Bible story using only 5 emojis. Make the group guess.
steps: Each player picks a Bible story and draws 5 emojis (with a pen, on paper) that tell it in order.
Pass papers around. Everyone tries to guess each story from the emojis.
After all guesses: the artist reveals the story and explains their choices.
games.why: Compressing a story to 5 symbols forces you to find its essence. Often a surprise — the emoji you chose for the climax tells you what you actually believe the story is about.

games.t: PARABLE PITCH · Sell It Like a Startup
games.h: Pitch the Good Samaritan to investors. Tagline, hook, ask.
steps: In small groups, each picks a parable. They have 8 minutes to prepare a Shark Tank-style pitch.
Pitch must include: a 1-sentence tagline, the "problem" the parable solves, the "ask" (what the audience should do).
Each group presents in 60 seconds. The room votes the most compelling pitch.
games.why: Forces you to identify what the parable is selling. Once you can pitch it, you understand it.

games.t: DIRECTOR'S CUT · Read with Direction
games.h: One reader. One director. The reader does everything the director says — angry, weepy, screaming.
steps: Pick a passage with dialogue (Job's laments, Jesus and Peter, David's psalms).
One person reads. Another is the Director, calling out emotions: "angry! whispering! desperate! triumphant!"
The reader must shift on every cue mid-sentence.
Rotate every 1-2 minutes.
games.why: Discovering that scripture has so many possible TONES is itself a revelation. Most of us read everything in the same monotone.

games.t: CASTING CALL · Hollywood Bible
games.h: You're directing a Bible biopic. Who plays Moses? Who plays Mary? Defend your cast.
steps: Pick a Bible story with multiple characters. Each person privately casts the roles using real-life celebrities, athletes, or family members.
Going around, share your full cast — with one-sentence justifications.
Group votes for the most surprising or fitting choice for each role.
games.why: Casting forces you to think about character traits. Why did you pick the soft-voiced actor for Mary? You'll discover what you actually think Mary was like.

games.t: ONE-MINUTE SERMON · 60 Seconds, Random Verse
games.h: Draw a verse from a bowl. Preach it. Sixty seconds. Go.
steps: Write 20 verse references on slips of paper. Put them in a bowl.
Each person draws one. They have 60 seconds to think. Then 60 seconds to "preach" on that verse.
No bailing. No "I don't know this one." Even if you only know one word — preach that word.
Group claps after each. No critique.
games.why: Forces you to find SOMETHING in a verse you've never thought about. Often the best insights come from total cold starts.

games.t: THE INVISIBLE PROP · Mime the Bible
games.h: Mime carrying biblical objects. Group guesses what.
steps: Pre-list 15 biblical objects: ark of the covenant, jar of oil, Goliath's sword, manger, scroll, fishing net, donkey, water jug, crown of thorns.
One person picks one and mimes carrying it across the room — how heavy is it, how wide, what shape.
Group guesses. Three guesses, then reveal.
Bonus: act out the action you'd do with it.
games.why: Forces you to think about scale and weight. The ark wasn't small. The crown of thorns wasn't a sweet halo. Embodiment teaches.

games.t: CAVE WALLS · Story in Six Panels
games.h: Draw a Bible story on the wall in 6 panels. No words allowed.
steps: Each person picks a Bible story and gets a piece of paper folded into 6 panels.
Draw the story in 6 sequential drawings. No words, no captions.
Pass papers around. Others try to identify the story and explain what they think is happening in each panel.
games.why: Stick figures are fine. The point: you find the climax by deciding which panel deserves to be the climax. That choice teaches.

games.t: PROPHET FOR A DAY · A Day in the Sandals
games.h: You woke up as Jeremiah. Walk us through your morning.
steps: Each person picks a prophet — Jeremiah, Isaiah, Hosea, Elijah, Jonah, Amos.
They describe a Tuesday in the prophet's life — getting up, what they ate, what God said to them, who hated them today, what they cried about.
Make it specific and ordinary. The big moments lived inside ordinary days.
games.why: Prophets were people. People had bad breath and routine. The drama of scripture happens in the middle of laundry.

games.t: WEDDING AT CANA · Modernize It
games.h: Tell the wedding-at-Cana story like it happened at your cousin's wedding last summer.
steps: Pick a miracle or scene. In small groups, retell it as if it happened in a modern setting — a cousin's wedding, a coffee shop, a high school cafeteria.
Each group performs a 2-minute skit.
Keep all the spiritual beats. Just change the setting.
games.why: Updating the setting forces you to ask what would feel actually miraculous today. That's where worship starts.

games.t: BIBLE BAND · Pick a Genre, Sing the Verse
games.h: Sing John 3:16 as country. Then metal. Then opera. Watch the verse mutate.
steps: Pick a verse everyone knows.
Each person picks a music genre — country, opera, rap, reggae, polka, lullaby, death metal.
Sing the verse in that genre, all the way through.
Round-robin. The group claps for each performance.
games.why: Different genres reveal different sides of the same verse. Country John 3:16 is mournful. Reggae John 3:16 is celebratory. Both are true.

games.t: THE OTHER GUY · Villain POV
games.h: Tell David and Goliath from Goliath's view. Or Easter from Pilate's.
steps: Pick a story with a clear antagonist — Goliath, Pharaoh, Pilate, Judas, the rich young ruler.
In small groups, retell the story from THEIR perspective. What were they thinking? What did they justify?
Each group performs 2-minute monologues.
After: what about their view did you understand for the first time?
games.why: Empathy for the villain is dangerous and necessary. You're more like Pharaoh than David more days than you'd admit.

games.t: SCROLL MAKER · Write a Lost Gospel
games.h: Imagine a "Gospel of Andrew" was found. Co-write a chapter together.
steps: Pick an under-known disciple — Andrew, Bartholomew, Thaddeus, Junia.
Pass a notebook around. Each person adds one paragraph to a "Gospel of [name]."
Stay true to the voice and theology of the New Testament. Don't go off the rails.
Read the finished chapter aloud at the end.
games.why: You can't write in a biblical voice without internalizing the actual biblical voice. The exercise teaches you what scripture sounds like by making you imitate it.

games.t: INTERVIEW WITH A FISH · Jonah's Whale Answers
games.h: The great fish gives a tell-all interview. The group asks anything.
steps: One person plays the great fish. They sit in a chair. They have to answer in-character — what was it like to swallow Jonah? Did he taste bad? Was God's voice scary?
The group asks any question.
Rotate the fish every 5 minutes. Try other characters: balaam's donkey, the rooster that crowed at Peter, the dove from Noah's ark.
games.why: Comedy unlocks empathy. By the end, the rooster has a real grievance about Peter. People remember the story forever.

games.t: PSALMS REMIX · Modern English Rewrite
games.h: Rewrite Psalm 23 like a text from God. Send it.
steps: Pick a psalm — short ones work well (23, 27, 121).
Rewrite it in the most modern language possible. Texts. Tweets. Instagram captions. Voice memos.
Share your version. Vote on the one that hits hardest.
After: read the original again. Different ear, different verse.
games.why: Translation is interpretation. You discover what each line REALLY means when you have to say it in your own words.

games.t: ANGELS UNAWARES · Improv with a Secret
games.h: One of you is an angel. The others don't know. Improv a scene.
steps: Write roles on paper: 1 angel, the rest humans. Hand out face-down.
Set a scene: a coffee shop, a family dinner, a homeless shelter, a long car ride.
Everyone improvises the scene. The angel's job: deliver one secret message during the scene without revealing they're an angel.
After: did anyone guess? When did the message land?
games.why: Hebrews 13:2 in practice. After this game, people pay more attention to strangers.

games.t: KINGDOM DREAMS · Heaven in Five Senses
games.h: Describe heaven using only smells, sounds, and textures. No clichés.
steps: Each person writes a description of heaven using only the five senses. No "streets of gold" — get specific.
What does it smell like? What sound do you hear when you wake up there? What does the air feel like on your skin?
Read your descriptions aloud. Notice how different they are.
games.why: Heaven is usually abstract. Forcing senses makes it concrete. People share things they didn't know they were longing for.

games.t: VERSE-LIBS · Mad Libs Meets Scripture
games.h: Plug nouns and verbs into a famous verse. Read it back. Try not to cry laughing.
steps: Pre-write a few verses with blanks. Example: 'For God so [verb] the [noun], that he gave his only [noun]...'
Without telling anyone the verse, ask the group for the words: 'Give me a verb. Now a noun. Now another noun.'
Fill the blanks in front of the group. Read the new "verse" out loud.
After the laughter: read the actual verse and notice how the right words feel like the only words.
games.why: Comedy makes you really see the original. The contrast is the point.

games.t: THE NAMING · Speed Recall
games.h: One topic. Sixty seconds. Name as many as you can.
steps: Pick a category: kings of Israel, women named in the New Testament, miracles of Jesus, books of the Bible in order.
Set a 60-second timer. Everyone writes down as many as they can — privately.
Reveal answers one at a time around the circle. You only score a point if no one else has it.
Most points after 5 categories wins.
games.why: Competition surfaces what you actually remember. The category that empties everyone's notebook is the one you should study next.

games.t: BIBLE BOGGLE · Words in the Grid
games.h: A 4x4 grid of letters. Find biblical words. Three minutes.
steps: Draw a 4x4 grid. Fill it randomly with letters (you can pull letters from a bag or use Scrabble tiles).
Set a 3-minute timer.
Everyone writes biblical words they find by connecting adjacent letters (vertically, horizontally, diagonally). Each letter only once per word.
Score: 3 letters = 1 point, 4 letters = 2 points, 5 = 3 points, 6+ = 5 points. Bonus +2 if no one else found it.
games.why: Quiet, fierce, and immediately fun. The kind of game where someone yells "JEHOVAH!" with too much enthusiasm.

games.t: WHO SAID IT? · Quote Attribution
games.h: Was it Solomon, Jesus, or Mark Twain? Place your bet.
steps: Pre-write 15 quotes on cards. Mix biblical quotes with famous secular quotes (Twain, Lincoln, song lyrics, movie quotes). Don't tell anyone the split.
Read each quote aloud. Everyone writes their guess: Bible, or Not Bible.
Reveal answers one at a time. Tally points.
The reveal is half the game — people are SHOCKED by which ones are biblical.
games.why: Scripture has shaped the way English speaks more than most people realize. This game makes that visible.

games.t: GENESIS COUNT · How Many ____ Are There?
games.h: Guess the number. Closest wins. Bonus: you actually learn it.
steps: Pre-research 8-10 'how many' questions. Examples: how many books in the Bible? How many psalms? How many words in John 3:16? How many days did Jesus appear after the resurrection?
Ask each question. Everyone writes a number.
Reveal the answer. Closest guess (above OR below) wins the point.
games.why: You'll never forget the answer once you've committed a wild guess to paper. The shame of guessing 700 books in the Bible cements 66 forever.

games.t: PSALM ACROSTIC · One Letter at a Time
games.h: Pick a word. Write a prayer where each line starts with the next letter.
steps: Each person picks a word — their name, a feeling, a theme like GRATITUDE or FORGIVE.
Write a short prayer where each LINE starts with the next letter of that word.
Read your acrostic out loud to the group when you're done.
games.why: Psalm 119 is an acrostic. So is much of Lamentations. You're using an actual biblical poetic form.

games.t: PROPHECY PUZZLE · Cryptic Riddles
games.h: A riddle hides a Bible character. Can you crack it?
steps: Pre-write 6-8 cryptic riddles, each describing a Bible character or place. Examples: "I sailed with the wind in my belly and found God in the dark." (Jonah). "My hair betrayed me before my eyes did." (Samson).
Read each riddle. Everyone writes their guess.
Reveal — point per correct answer. Bonus point for explaining the clue best.
games.why: Solving forces you to see characters as collections of details, not labels. Memory gets sticky.

games.t: PARABLE CONNECTIONS · Match the Meaning
games.h: A parable on this card. A truth on that card. Find the pair.
steps: Pre-write 6-8 parable cards (just the parable name or a one-line summary) and 6-8 truth cards (the parable's point — "humility before God", "the value of one lost soul", etc).
Shuffle and spread face-up.
Race to match parables to truths. Discuss any disagreements — sometimes a parable means more than one thing.
games.why: Hard mode: more than one truth can fit a parable. That ambiguity IS the lesson.

games.t: NINE GENERATIONS · Memory Chain
games.h: Adam begat Seth, who begat Enosh, who begat... your turn.
steps: Pick a genealogy — Genesis 5, Matthew 1, Luke 3. Look it up beforehand so the moderator can verify.
Going around the circle, each person says the next name in the line.
If you miss, you're out. Last person standing wins.
Variation: do it backwards.
games.why: The Bible takes its genealogies seriously. Spending 10 minutes recalling them changes how you read them. They become real people, not skim-past lists.

games.t: TEN COMMANDMENTS RACE · Speed Memory
games.h: Recite all ten in order in under 60 seconds. Solo or relay.
steps: Solo: stand up, recite all 10 commandments in order. Time it. Beat your own time.
Relay: each team member says one commandment in order. If anyone fumbles or hesitates, the team restarts. First team done wins.
After: which one always slips? Usually 'remember the Sabbath' or 'do not covet.'
games.why: Most Christians can't recite all ten. Most can after one round of this game.

games.t: ABRAHAMIC CHAIN · Down the Line
games.h: Abraham. Isaac. Jacob. The chain keeps going. Don't break it.
steps: Pick a line of biblical succession — patriarchs, judges, kings of Israel, kings of Judah, apostles.
Going around the circle, each person says the next name in order.
Miss = sit out. Last person standing wins.
Run it 3 times — different chain each time.
games.why: By round 3 you've internalized three biblical lineages. Free Bible nerd points.

games.t: BIBLE TRIVIA SHOWDOWN · Tournament
games.h: Bracket-style 1v1 trivia. Last person standing claims the throne.
steps: Pre-write 30+ trivia questions across difficulty levels.
Bracket pair-ups. Each match: 3 questions, fastest correct answer wins.
Winners advance. Losers form a "loser's bracket" with their own crown.
Final: champion of bracket vs. champion of loser's bracket.
games.why: Competition over content. Everyone learns even when they lose.

games.t: ALL THE WAY THROUGH · 66 Books in Order
games.h: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus... can you make it to Revelation?
steps: Solo or relay: name all 66 books of the Bible in order without stopping.
Time it. Try to beat your time.
Group mode: each person says ONE book in order, going around. Miss = team restarts.
games.why: By the third try, the order finally sticks. Suddenly you can find Habakkuk.

games.t: PSALMS SCAVENGER · 60-Second Verse Hunt
games.h: Find a verse about [topic] in 60 seconds. Go.
steps: Everyone needs a Bible (paper or app).
Leader calls a topic: courage, grief, kindness, anger, parenting, work.
Each person has 60 seconds to find a verse on that topic and bookmark/note it.
Going around, share your verse and one sentence about why you picked it.
games.why: Topical scripture-hunting builds the muscle of 'I know where to find help.' Lifesaving skill.

games.t: SACRED ANAGRAMS · Unscramble the Name
games.h: SCAEELN = ELEAZAR. Solve the Bible name from the jumble.
steps: Pre-write 10-15 Bible names as anagrams on cards.
Reveal one at a time. First to shout the correct name gets the point.
Bonus point if you can name one thing the person did.
games.why: Forces letter-by-letter familiarity with names you usually skim. The "obscure" names become familiar.

games.t: WHOSE BIRTHRIGHT? · Match Story to Character
games.h: Card says "sold his birthright for soup." Who? GO.
steps: Pre-write 15-20 short story descriptions on cards (1 sentence each).
Reveal one at a time. First to name the character correctly scores.
Tiebreaker: name what happened next.
games.why: Forces story recall, not just name recognition. Different kind of Bible knowledge.

games.t: NUMBERS GAME · What Happened in 40?
games.h: I say a number. You tell me what it means in scripture.
steps: Leader calls out a number: 7, 12, 40, 144, 666, 153, 70, 3.
Players race to name what that number signifies in the Bible. First correct answer scores.
Multiple right answers possible — keep listing until no one has more.
games.why: Biblical numerology is real. Knowing the symbolic weights of 7 (perfection), 40 (testing), 12 (tribes/apostles) deepens every passage.

games.t: PROVERBS RACE · Finish the Line
games.h: "A soft answer turns away..." Quick! Finish it!
steps: Leader reads the first half of a Proverb. Players race to finish it (paraphrase OK).
Correct finish = point. Wrong = the opportunity passes around the room.
Run through 15-20 proverbs.
games.why: Proverbs become a vocabulary you carry. The book stops feeling like a fortune cookie and starts feeling like a toolkit.

games.t: APOSTLE MATCH · Twelve Plus Paul
games.h: Match each apostle to their fact: who was a tax collector? Who doubted? Who walked on water?
steps: Pre-write 12 apostles on cards. Pre-write 12 facts on other cards. Shuffle.
Race to match apostle to fact. First all-correct wins.
Bonus round: order them by who died first/last (Judas, James, Peter etc).
games.why: Most Christians can name 4-6 apostles. After this game, all 12 are distinct people.

games.t: PARABLE DECODER · Cryptic Clues
games.h: "A small seed becomes a tree." Which parable?
steps: Pre-write cryptic 1-line clues for parables: "A reckless father throws a party for a quitter" = Prodigal Son.
Read each clue. First to name the parable scores.
Bonus: name the chapter of Matthew, Mark, or Luke it's in.
games.why: Forces you to see the parable through its symbolic content, not its title.

games.t: CONCORDANCE CHAOS · Race to the Verse
games.h: I say a verse. You find it FAST. Old testament harder. Go.
steps: Everyone has a Bible (paper preferred).
Leader calls a reference: "Galatians 5:22-23!" Everyone races to find it and stand up when ready.
First standing reads it aloud. Point per win.
Mix in obscure books: Habakkuk, Obadiah, Zephaniah, 3 John.
games.why: Speed-finding Bible references is a vanishing skill. This makes it competitive and fun. Younger group members get GOOD fast.

games.t: BIBLE BINGO · Free-Form 5x5
games.h: Each square is a Bible theme or character. Cross them off as they appear.
steps: Hand out blank 5x5 grids. Each player fills theirs with Bible characters or themes (free choice).
Leader reads short Bible passages or trivia clues.
Players cross off matching squares.
First to 5 in a row wins.
games.why: Listening becomes active. Every passage suddenly has stakes for someone.

games.t: RIDDLE OF JESUS · Decipher His Sayings
games.h: "The first shall be last." What did He mean? Defend your read.
steps: Pre-pick 5-7 cryptic things Jesus said: "Let the dead bury their dead." "I came not to bring peace but a sword." "Take up your cross."
For each saying, the group debates what it means. No phones — only memory and shared opinion.
After: open the verse, read the surrounding context. See whose interpretation was closest.
games.why: Jesus was a master of riddle and paradox. Wrestling with the saying BEFORE looking up "the right answer" teaches honest reading.

games.t: NAME THAT KING · Match the Dynasty
games.h: Was he good? Was he bad? Which dad? Quick — who is he?
steps: Pre-write 10-15 cards with one-line king bios: "Killed by his son Absalom's rebellion" (David). "Asked for wisdom" (Solomon). "Rebuilt the temple" (Hezekiah).
Race to name the king. Point per correct answer.
Bonus: name the parent and the kid.
games.why: Israel and Judah's kings blur together unless you build distinct mental hooks for each one. This game builds them.

games.t: CHAPTER COUNT · How Long Is It?
games.h: How many chapters in Genesis? Isaiah? Jude? Closest wins.
steps: Leader names a Bible book. Everyone writes their guess for # of chapters.
Reveal answer. Closest (above OR below) wins the point.
Run through 10-15 books. Mix big (Psalms = 150) and tiny (Obadiah = 1).
games.why: Suddenly you have a mental map of the Bible. You know Jude is short and Isaiah is long without having to check.

games.t: HOT SEAT · One Chair, Any Question
games.h: You sit. The group asks anything for 3 minutes. You answer honestly.
steps: Set one chair facing the group. One person sits in it.
For 3 minutes (timed), the group asks anything — about faith, life, fears, joys, doubts.
The hot-seat person can pass on any question with 'next.' No follow-up explanation required.
Everyone rotates. Whole group does the chair.
games.why: Trust grows in the spaces where we don't have to perform answers. This game creates that space.

games.t: WOULD YOU RATHER · Bible Edition
games.h: Two impossible choices. Pick one. Defend yourself.
steps: Pre-write 10-15 Bible-themed 'would you rather' questions. Examples: 'Would you rather be Jonah in the fish or Daniel in the lions' den?' 'Cross the Red Sea or witness the empty tomb?' 'Have Solomon's wisdom or David's heart?'
Read each one. Everyone picks a side — point or stand to represent it.
Two volunteers from each side defend their choice. 30 seconds each.
No "winner" — just listening to the reasons.
games.why: Forcing a binary surfaces the things you actually value. The defending part is where you discover what you didn't know you believed.

games.t: STORY CIRCLE · One Word at a Time
games.h: Tell a Bible story, but each person can only add one word.
steps: Pick a Bible story you all know roughly — Noah's ark, David and Goliath, the lost coin.
Going around the circle, each person says ONE word at a time, building the story together.
No conferring. Take what's given. Stay in the story.
Stop when the story reaches its natural end. Then talk about how the story shifted compared to the real one.
games.why: The story comes out weird, then surprisingly profound. Each word reveals what each person remembers, prioritizes, hears.

games.t: THE FISHBOWL · Inner Ring, Outer Ring
games.h: Five people talk. The rest listen. Then the rings switch.
steps: Set 5 chairs in an inner circle. The rest of the group sits in an outer ring around them.
The inner circle discusses a topic — a passage, a question, a controversy — for 10 minutes. The outer ring listens silently.
After 10 minutes, swap. Inner ring goes outer; outer becomes inner. They pick up the thread.
After both rounds: full group discussion of what they noticed about how the conversation shifted.
games.why: Listening without being able to interrupt is a forgotten skill. You hear deeper. The second ring builds on the first.

games.t: DESERT ISLAND VERSE · Defend Your One
games.h: Stranded for a year. You get one verse. Which one? Why?
steps: Each person picks one Bible verse they would take with them if they could only have one for the rest of their life.
Going around, share the verse and explain why — what's happened in your life that makes that verse the one?
Others can ask one question to dig deeper, but no debate.
Optional: write everyone's verse on a piece of paper, photograph, send around as the group's 'wall' of verses.
games.why: You'll never know your group at the level of "one verse." This is how to find out.

games.t: TIME TRAVELER · Tell Your Younger Self
games.h: If you could send one Bible truth to 12-year-old you, what would it be?
steps: Each person thinks of an age in their past — 10, 15, 21, the moment before a big decision.
Share: what biblical truth do you wish you'd known then? What would you tell yourself?
Others listen, then offer one verse that they think speaks to that moment in your life.
Save them. Group will leave with a personal verse collection.
games.why: The intersection of biblical truth and personal history is where Scripture stops being abstract.

games.t: WORST CASE BLESSING · The Hidden Hand
games.h: Share your worst chapter. The group helps you find where God was in it.
steps: Each person shares ONE hard season from their life. 3 minutes max. No advice, no fixing.
After they share, others reflect back: where do you see God's hand in this story? What scripture comes to mind?
The sharer doesn't have to agree — they just listen.
Next person.
games.why: Romans 8:28 is easy to quote. This game is how a group lives it — together, with someone's real pain on the table.

games.t: THE LAST WORD · End on a Verse
games.h: Everyone picks a verse that captures tonight. Read them in turn to close.
steps: At the end of a Bible study, give the group 3 minutes to find or recall a verse that captures something from the night — a feeling, a question, a hope.
Going around, each person reads their verse and says one sentence about why.
Don't comment in between. Just let each verse hang in the air.
games.why: Closing rituals are sticky. The verse each person picks becomes their personal stamp on the night.

games.t: SUNDAY OBSERVATIONS · Round Robin Noticing
games.h: Each person names one thing they noticed in the passage. Nothing more.
steps: Pick a passage. Read it together — twice, slowly.
Going around, each person says ONE thing they noticed. Could be a word, a contradiction, a question, an emotion.
No commentary on others' observations. Just receive.
After everyone's shared, open it up for discussion. You'll have 8-12 entry points instead of one.
games.why: Most studies follow the loudest person. This game makes sure the quietest person speaks first.

games.t: GRATITUDE LADDER · Build Each Other Up
games.h: Going around, each person names one thing they appreciate about the next.
steps: Sit in a circle. Going clockwise, each person says one specific thing they appreciate about the person to their left.
Not generic ('you're great') — specific ('the way you stayed after to help clean up last week made me feel less alone').
Receive without deflecting. Just say thank you.
Go all the way around. Everyone gives, everyone receives.
games.why: Encouragement is muscle the modern world atrophies. This game flexes it. The group leaves taller than they came in.

games.t: ONE-WORD SUNDAY · This Week Was...
games.h: One word for the week. No follow-up. Just the word.
steps: Around the circle, each person says ONE word that describes their week. Anything.
Listen without responding.
Optional second pass: anyone who wants to says a verse that came to mind for someone else's word.
games.why: A status check that respects introverts. Everyone gets heard, no one has to explain.

games.t: WHAT GOD TOLD ME · Recent Whispers
games.h: What's one thing God has nudged you on lately? Share, don't justify.
steps: Each person shares one thing they sense God has been pressing on them recently.
Could be a verse, a feeling, a recurring thought, a stranger's comment.
Others listen, then pray briefly for that nudge.
games.why: Naming the nudge is half of obeying it. The group becomes witnesses.

games.t: UNFINISHED VERSE · The One You Can't Get Past
games.h: Which verse have you been stuck on for years? Confess it.
steps: Each person names a verse they've never been able to fully accept, understand, or live out.
Share one sentence about why.
Others reflect — what helps them with it, or what about it troubles them too.
games.why: Honest about the verses you struggle with = honest about your actual faith. Most people are relieved someone else struggles too.

games.t: PROVERB SWAP · One I Live, One I Fight
games.h: A proverb you LIVE by. A proverb you can't stand. Share both.
steps: Each person picks two proverbs: one they live by, one they wrestle with.
Share both. Brief explanation each.
Others can ask one clarifying question. No debate.
games.why: Proverbs is dismissed as platitudes. This game lets it become wisdom you wear and wisdom you resist.

games.t: PSALM OF GRIEF · Name Your Sorrow
games.h: Name one sorrow. Anchor it to a psalm. The group bears it with you.
steps: Each person names one current or recent grief. Two sentences max.
Then: 'The psalm that meets me here is ___.' Say the reference and read or recall a line.
Group sits in silence for 10 seconds, then says: 'We bear it with you.'
Next person.
games.why: Naming grief out loud, in scripture's language, with witnesses, lifts weight you didn't know you were carrying. Sacred work.

games.t: THE BLESSING ROUND · Speak Over Them
games.h: Going clockwise. Speak a one-line blessing over the person to your left.
steps: Sit in a circle. Going clockwise, each person speaks a blessing over the person to their left.
Format: "May God ___ over you this year."
Specific is better than general. 'May God give you peace' is fine. 'May God shut the mouths of the people who underestimate you' is better.
Receive in silence. Just say thank you when you're blessed.
games.why: Speaking blessing is the oldest priestly act. After this game, the group feels different — like they belong to each other.

games.t: THE WALKING CONVERSATION · Walk and Talk
games.h: Pair up. Walk for 15 minutes. Talk about one question. No phones.
steps: Pair up. Step outside (or walk around the building).
Each pair gets one question to discuss while walking: "Where are you sensing God this season?" "What scripture is meeting you lately?"
Walk for 12-15 minutes. Return.
Optional: in the big group, each person shares one thing their partner said.
games.why: Walking lowers defenses. Side-by-side conversation is deeper than face-to-face. You'll get more out of one walk than three sit-downs.

games.t: PRAYER REQUEST RELAY · Pass It Right
games.h: Share a prayer request. The person to your right prays for you, out loud, now.
steps: Going clockwise. Each person shares one prayer request out loud.
The person to their right immediately prays for them. Out loud. Right now. Short.
Then THAT person shares their request. The next person prays. And so on.
games.why: Prayer for each other becomes specific and immediate, not 'I'll add you to my list.' Builds the muscle of praying for someone in real time.

games.t: WHAT YOU'D ASK GOD · One Question
games.h: Sit with God for 60 seconds. One question only. What is it?
steps: Each person sits in silence for 60 seconds, thinking: if I had ONE question for God, what would it be?
Going around, each person says their question.
No one tries to answer it for them. Just receive.
Optional: pray together that God would meet each question.
games.why: Your real question reveals your real faith. The unspoken question is heavier than any sermon.

games.t: WHEN GOD WAS QUIET · The Wilderness Season
games.h: Share a season when God felt silent. What got you through?
steps: Each person names one season — a year, a stretch — when God felt silent or absent.
What got you through? A person? A verse? A song? A stubborn refusal to quit?
Others listen, then offer one thing they were inspired by.
games.why: Silence from God is universal, rarely talked about. This game ends the loneliness of those seasons.

games.t: THE GOSPEL IN MY LIFE · Hits Different Today
games.h: The gospel you grew up with vs. the gospel that's meeting you now. What's changed?
steps: Each person shares: which part of the gospel hits hardest for you right now? Is it the same as when you were 18? Different from a year ago?
What's emphasized in your understanding today? What's quieter?
Listen. The shape of someone's gospel reveals their season.
games.why: The gospel hits differently at different ages. Naming the shift is naming where you are with God.

games.t: FAITH STORY · Three Minute Autobiography
games.h: Your whole faith story in 3 minutes. Pick the three moments that matter.
steps: Each person tells their faith story in 3 minutes flat. Time it.
Pick the three moments that mattered most — not all the details.
After all stories, point: what was a moment that landed for you in someone else's?
games.why: Most groups never hear each other's stories. This sets the floor for everything after.

games.t: JESUS WOULD HAVE LAUGHED · Find the Humor
games.h: Where is the comedy in scripture? Find a passage that's actually funny.
steps: Each person finds a Bible passage they think is genuinely funny. (Hint: Elijah mocking the prophets of Baal, Jonah arguing with God about a plant, Peter cutting an ear off.)
Share it. Explain why you think it's funny.
Others laugh. Or argue. Discuss.
games.why: The Bible is funnier than we give it credit. Recovering the humor recovers the humanity of the people in it.

games.t: HARDEST VERSE · The One You Resist
games.h: Name the verse you most want to skip. Explain why.
steps: Each person names a verse they struggle with — the one they want to disagree with, the one that troubles them, the one they don't fully believe.
Share why. No fixing each other.
Optional: pray that the verse would somehow become hospitable over time.
games.why: Honest about resistance = real about faith. Group bonds over shared wrestling, not shared comfort.

games.t: NEXT CHAPTER · Where Is God Leading?
games.h: If God were writing your next chapter, what's the title?
steps: Each person writes a title for their next 'chapter' of life. Three words max.
Share titles. Explain in one sentence.
Group prays a 30-second prayer over each person's titled chapter.
games.why: Naming the next season makes it real. Giving it a title makes it shareable. Praying over it makes it sacred.

games.t: TWO TRUTHS AND A BIBLE LIE
games.h: They'll never guess which one you made up. Probably.
steps: Each person says three statements: two from the Bible (real verses, events, characters) and one they made up that SOUNDS biblical.
The group guesses which one is the lie.
Bonus points if the lie sounds totally plausible. Extra bonus if a 'truth' sounds fake.
games.why: The Bible contains weirder true stories than we remember. You'll discover lies that turn out to be real (and real stuff you swore was a joke).

games.t: NAME + VERSE · I'm ___ and my verse is ___
games.h: Introduce yourself with the verse that defines your year.
steps: Around the circle, each person says: 'I'm [name], and my verse this year is [verse + brief reason].'
One sentence about why that verse, not a full testimony.
Listen for verses you've never heard. Listen for stories behind familiar verses.
games.why: You learn more about a person from their verse-of-the-year than from a 5-minute introduction. It's a window straight into where they are.

games.t: SAINT OR SINNER · Quick Character Moments
games.h: Draw a Bible character. Was their week a saint week or a sinner week? Defend.
steps: Write 12-15 Bible characters on slips of paper. Fold and put in a bowl.
Each person draws a slip. They have 30 seconds to argue whether that character had a "saint week" or "sinner week" in the Bible.
Group votes saint or sinner. Whoever wins the most rounds, wins.
The fun is that almost every character has both — you have to pick which moment to argue.
games.why: No one in Scripture is a flat hero or villain. This game makes you see characters in 3D.

games.t: ARK ABCs · I'm Packing My Ark...
games.h: Memory chain that gets harder every round. Watch the group sweat.
steps: First person says: 'I'm packing my ark and I'm taking an aardvark.' (Starts with A.)
Next person: 'I'm packing my ark and I'm taking an aardvark and a bear.'
Each person repeats the full list and adds the next letter of the alphabet.
Mess up, you're out. Group cheers anyway.
games.why: A classic memory game with a Bible frame. Disarms the room and gets everyone listening.

games.t: GOD'S TRAIL MIX · One Word For You
games.h: One word that describes you spiritually right now. Just one.
steps: Going around, each person says ONE word that describes where they are spiritually right now. Hungry. Wandering. Tired. Hopeful. Dry. Curious.
No explanation needed. Just the word.
After everyone's shared, the leader prays over the words.
games.why: One word is honest. One word lets the introverts speak as deeply as the extroverts.

games.t: BAPTISMAL NAME · Pick a Bible Name
games.h: If you had to take a Bible name, which one? Why?
steps: Each person picks a Bible name they'd adopt if they had to. Could be a hero, could be obscure (Eutychus, Tabitha, Onesimus).
Share the name and ONE sentence about why.
The group can't object — only ask, 'why that one?'
games.why: You learn what story someone sees themselves in. Often surprising — the loudest person picks the quietest character, or vice versa.

games.t: FIVE FINGERS · Things in Common
games.h: Find five things this whole group has in common. Anything goes.
steps: In small groups of 4-6, you have 5 minutes to find five things EVERY person in the group has in common.
Cannot be: "we're all human," "we're all here." Must be specific.
Examples: 'We've all been to a funeral this year.' 'We all played a team sport in high school.' 'We all have a sibling.' 'We all believe in prayer.'
Each group shares their five with the whole room.
games.why: Specificity creates intimacy. The deeper you go to find common ground, the closer the group gets.

games.t: ROOM SHAPED LIKE · Place Yourself
games.h: Imagine this room is a giant map of your week. Where do you stand?
steps: Tell the group: 'This room is a map. That corner is amazing, that corner is awful, that wall is exhausted, that wall is excited. Walk to where your week put you.'
Everyone walks to their spot. Look around.
Pick 3-4 people from different spots to say one sentence about why they're standing there.
games.why: A status check that takes 60 seconds and tells you exactly who needs to be checked in on later.

games.t: THE PROPHET NEXT DOOR · If I Were a Prophet...
games.h: If God called you to deliver a message to your city this week, what would it be?
steps: Around the circle: 'If you were a prophet and God called you to deliver one message to your city or workplace or family this week, what would the message be?'
Each person shares one sentence. Don't over-explain.
The group listens. Notice the patterns.
games.why: Forces clarity. The thing you would shout from a rooftop is the thing you actually believe matters most right now.

games.t: WALKING WITH PAUL · Three Questions
games.h: You get one walk with any Bible character. Three questions. Make them count.
steps: Each person picks a Bible character they'd take a walk with — anyone except Jesus.
Share: who you picked, and the three questions you'd ask.
The group can vote on whose questions are the most interesting.
games.why: Questions reveal more than answers. You'll learn what each person is wrestling with by what they'd ask.

games.t: SPIRITUAL ANIMAL · You as a Creature
games.h: If your spiritual life were an animal right now, what would it be?
steps: Each person names an animal that represents where they are spiritually. Bear hibernating? Eagle? Lost puppy? Newborn lamb?
Share the animal and one sentence about why.
Group laughs, group sees you.
games.why: The animal you pick tells the truth before your words can. Plus everyone's answer is memorable.

games.t: SEVEN DAYS · One Word Per Day
games.h: Monday through Sunday. One word each. Sum up the week.
steps: Each person says one word for each day of the past week.
Mon: tired. Tues: surprising. Wed: quiet. Thurs: hopeful. Fri: scared. Sat: blessed. Sun: full.
No explanations needed. Just listen.
games.why: You hear the shape of someone's week without the small talk. Surprisingly intimate.

games.t: PSALM I'D WRITE · One Line
games.h: If you wrote a psalm today, what's the first line?
steps: Each person thinks of the opening line of a psalm they'd write today.
Share. One sentence each.
Listen for the shared notes — gratitude, grief, longing.
games.why: Forces poetic compression. The line that comes out is more honest than a paragraph would be.

games.t: EMOJI TESTIMONY · Faith Story in 3 Emojis
games.h: Your whole faith story. Three emojis. Go.
steps: Each person draws or writes three emojis on paper that tell their faith story.
Reveal one at a time, explain each emoji's role.
The group can guess what each emoji means before you tell them.
games.why: Compression forces clarity. Three emojis is the right length to remember someone's story by next week.

games.t: THE CHAIR THAT CHOSE YOU · Why Did You Sit There?
games.h: Why did you pick THIS chair today? Defend your subconscious.
steps: Going around, each person says: 'I picked this chair because ___.'
Could be: close to the door, far from the loud guy, next to my friend, the only empty one, the one in the light.
Notice patterns. Laugh at yourselves.
games.why: Reveals social truths everyone knows but never names. Light and disarming.

games.t: WORK-WEEK WIN · Brag + Verse
games.h: One win from your week. One verse that fits.
steps: Each person shares one win from their week — work, family, personal.
Then names a verse that fits the moment.
Doesn't have to be deep. Could be silly.
games.why: Bragging is hard for Christians. This game makes it spiritual — turning ordinary wins into thanksgiving.

games.t: GIDEON FLEECE · An If-Then
games.h: If you laid out a fleece this week — "God, if X, then Y" — what would X be?
steps: Each person shares a real "if-then" they're wrestling with: "If God provides this job, I'll do Y." "If God shows me a sign, I'll trust them."
Not necessarily plans — just the unspoken bargaining most of us do.
Group listens. No advice.
games.why: Naming the fleece is naming the doubt. Surprisingly often, just saying it out loud dissolves it.

games.t: SECOND-FAVORITE VERSE · Beyond John 3:16
games.h: Not your go-to. Your second. The deep cut.
steps: Each person names their SECOND-favorite verse — the deep cut, the one they reach for when no one's watching.
Share why.
Notice: the second-favorites are usually more honest than the first-favorites.
games.why: First favorites are public-facing. Second favorites are private. Game gets you behind the curtain.

games.t: APP OF YOUR HEART · What Gets the Hour?
games.h: Apps tell on us. Which app got most of your time this week?
steps: Each person admits which app or activity got the most of their time this week.
No shaming. Just naming.
Optional: as a group, briefly pray about it.
games.why: Where your time goes is where your worship goes. This game makes that visible without lecturing.

games.t: PSALM 23 LINE · Pick Your Favorite
games.h: The most famous psalm. Which line is YOURS?
steps: Read Psalm 23 together (or have everyone open it).
Each person picks the line that's most theirs RIGHT NOW.
Share the line and one sentence about why.
games.why: The same psalm meets different people differently in different seasons. Visible map of where the group is.

games.t: JESUS WALKED IN · What Would He Notice?
games.h: Jesus walks into your kitchen tonight. What does He see?
steps: Each person imagines Jesus physically walking into their home tonight.
What does He notice first? What does He say? What does He do?
Share. The specificity matters.
games.why: Putting Jesus into your real space makes Him stop being abstract. Suddenly the dishes matter and so does the open Bible on the table.

games.t: BIBLICAL SUPERPOWER · Pick One
games.h: Walk on water. Heal the sick. Part the sea. Pick ONE. Why?
steps: Each person picks one biblical 'power' they'd want for a day: walking on water, multiplying food, healing, parting seas, raising the dead, prophesying, walking through walls.
Share which and why.
Notice what each person's pick says about what they wish they could solve.
games.why: What you wish for reveals what you're carrying. Light game, deep answers.

games.t: ADJECTIVE NAME · Joyful Joel
games.h: Your name with a Bible-flavored adjective starting with the same letter.
steps: Each person gives themselves a Bible-adjacent adjective that starts with the same letter as their name: Joyful Joel, Patient Pat, Steady Sarah, Faithful Frank.
Going around, each person says THEIR name AND repeats everyone's before them.
Miss = funny consequence (silly dance, etc).
games.why: Memorable, silly, gets everyone's name into the room twice. Classic for a reason.

games.t: WHAT'S IN YOUR BACKPACK · Spiritual Baggage
games.h: You're carrying invisible stuff into this room. Name one item.
steps: Each person 'unpacks' one invisible thing they brought into the room tonight.
Could be: a hard conversation from earlier, a worry about tomorrow, a recent loss, a hope.
No fixing. Just naming.
games.why: Names the unspoken context that's otherwise running quietly in the background of the study.

games.t: ROOM TEMPERATURE · Hot, Cold, or Lukewarm?
games.h: Revelation 3:16-style self-check. Hot, cold, or lukewarm right now?
steps: Going around, each person says: 'My faith temperature right now is ___' — hot, cold, lukewarm, frozen, simmering.
Optional: one sentence about why.
No judgment from the group.
games.why: Forces self-honesty using scripture's own language. People often confess “lukewarm” out loud for the first time.
